site.title: Dr. Sean Tobin
site.tagline: Seeking wholeness and holiness in the age of AI.
site.intro: I'm a clinical psychologist and Catholic author. I write about healing, humanity, and the interior life: integration in a world increasingly fragmented. The Inner Exodus is the way through.
site.irenaeus: The glory of God is man fully alive, and the life of man is the vision of God.

bio: I am fascinated by the human person. By what we love, why we suffer, how we find meaning, and what it actually takes to heal and grow. I'm a clinical psychologist by training, and creative and contemplative by disposition, more interested in people than in theories about them.

Most of my work comes down to one question: how do you stay a whole person in a world built to pull you apart? I sit with people in the ordinary wreckage of that, the anxiety, the distraction, the sense of being scattered across a hundred screens, and help them come home to themselves.

I also believe artificial intelligence is the defining shift of our lifetime, and I don't think the response is to stand outside it and worry. I've spent the last few years becoming fluent in it: building tools and systems, testing where it helps and where it harms, and asking how technology can serve human formation rather than erode it. That intersection of the human person and the machine is where I most want to work, as a psychologist, a writer, and increasingly a builder.

I came to all of it the long way. I was an atheist for years and found faith slowly, through my questions rather than around them. I'm Catholic now, and it's the deepest layer of how I understand the person, though you don't need to share it to find something real here. Most of my thinking lands first in The Inner Exodus. Whether you came for the psychology, the technology, the faith, or just a sense that modern life is costing us more than we admit, I'm glad you're here.

books.title: Remaining Human
books.subtitle: A plain-language companion to Pope Leo XIV's encyclical on AI
books.description: A readable guide to Magnifica Humanitas: what artificial intelligence is doing to attention, desire, and the soul, and how the Church calls us to remain fully human as the machines arrive.
long: Remaining Human is my plain-language companion to Magnifica Humanitas, Pope Leo XIV's encyclical on artificial intelligence. I am Dr. Sean Tobin, a clinical psychologist and Catholic author. The Church has spoken directly into what these machines are doing to us, and most people will never read the document. This book opens it up: what the Holy Father actually says, why he says it, and what it asks of an ordinary person living half their life through a screen. Available in paperback and Kindle.

The book follows the encyclical's own concerns: what AI is doing to attention, to desire, and to the soul. And what the Church means when she calls us to remain fully human while all of it arrives. No academic apparatus, no tech panic. A clear walk through a document written for people who are already living inside what it describes.

I wrote it as a clinical psychologist and a Catholic author, because that is the seam this shift runs along: the human person on one side, the machine on the other. The encyclical deserves to be opened up rather than summarized away. And what it asks is harder and simpler than a position on technology. It asks you to stay a person while you use it.

books.title: Big God, Little Devil
books.subtitle: A radical shift in the approach to spiritual warfare and deliverance
books.description: A psychologist's book on the demonic that refuses both obsession and denial: the devil is real, and he is small. A book about getting the proportions right, and getting free.
long: A few years into my clinical practice I started getting a referral that graduate school doesn't prepare you for: people who needed a psychological evaluation before an exorcist would pray over them. I am Dr. Sean Tobin, a clinical psychologist, and that chair is where this book comes from. I had already written my doctoral dissertation on exorcism, deliverance, and psychotherapy, mostly because the question was the one elephant in the room nobody in my program wanted to talk about, and then the referrals turned the research into a specialization. Big God, Little Devil is what I learned sitting there. Available in hardcover, paperback, Kindle, and audiobook.

One woman had been receiving exorcisms every other week for three years. Each one bought her a few days of peace, and then the thing would manifest again, heavier, in retaliation for her trying to get free. In one of the first evaluation sessions we stopped attending to the presence and went to the feeling underneath it instead, and a memory surfaced from childhood, the place where the helplessness first got in. She met the Lord inside that memory. The demon left and never came back. I watched some version of that happen too many times to keep filing it under exception.

The war is won. The enemy is disarmed. So why are so many Christians still living in fear? In a lot of places spiritual warfare has been twisted into a spectacle, and the spectacle breeds anxiety, superstition, and control. What I argue in this book is that deliverance is not about confrontation but communion, that we do not fight for victory so much as live from it, and that fear-based methods usually deepen the very thing they're trying to remove, because the moment your confidence sits in the technique rather than in the relationship, you have quietly gone back to a system of works.

So the book walks through why fear-based deliverance often makes the problem worse, how the Holy Spirit integrates what the enemy tried to fragment, how worship and testimony silence accusation, why trust rather than striving is the real battleground, and how the sacraments and Scripture equip an ordinary person to walk in peace and power. It is written for the battle-weary and the curious, for ministers and for the laypeople who have been told all of this sits above their authority. Fr. Boniface Hicks, OSB wrote the foreword. Dr. Mary Healy, who serves on the Pontifical Biblical Commission, calls it dynamite and believes it will help change the whole paradigm for the ministries of deliverance and exorcism.

The devil is real, and he is also small. Most of what I'm doing in these pages is putting those two facts back into proportion, because a soul that has the proportions right is already most of the way free.

books.title: Sick Seven
books.subtitle: A children's story about anxiety and presence
books.description: A picture book for kids about the worry that visits us all, and the quiet, steady presence that meets it. Gentle, funny, and true.
long: Sick Seven is a picture book about a number who gets sick on the inside. Not a cold, not a bug, just the particular sickness that comes from carrying too much worry and too much pressure to be good enough. I am Dr. Sean Tobin, a clinical psychologist, and I wrote it for the four to eight year olds who already know that feeling and don't have a word for it yet. Paperback and Kindle.

Seven doesn't get fixed by advice. Everybody on the street has a suggestion and keeps walking, which is roughly how it goes for a kid in distress. Then a quiet character shaped like a plus sign stops, sees him, and stays, and that turns out to be the whole medicine. Seven's color comes back. The last thing he does in the book is stop for somebody else.

Two things I've never admitted inside the book itself. The first is that it is the Good Samaritan. Everyone passes the one in the ditch until somebody stops, sees, stays, and then pays for what comes next, and that is the shape of the story, with a plus sign that happens to look like a cross doing the stopping. The second is that the title is a dad joke. My kids, like every kid in North America at the moment, cannot stop saying six seven at the dinner table, and I decided the correct response was to write an entire children's book about a sick seven and publish it. Writing a book is a long way to go for a joke, and I regret nothing.

Underneath the joke it is doing real clinical work. Kids learn that distress is not a defect to be fixed, that presence is what actually helps, and that they can be the one who stops. It reads aloud in about the length of a bedtime that's already running late.
